entries.name: Backgammon is played by two persons

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / The Board and Men / p. 271

entries.evidence: Backgammon is played by two persons, on a special "board" with thirty "men," fifteen white and fifteen black (or red), similar to those used for the game of Draughts.
entries.note: men-count took the thirty men from this sentence and left the two persons in it. The engine's Player type and every player-relative rule rest on the count; nothing mapped it.

entries.name: Thirty men, fifteen to a side

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / The Board and Men / p. 271

entries.evidence: Both figures.

entries.name: The board is two tables, inner and outer

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / The Board and Men / p. 272

entries.evidence: The board is so placed in use that the two compartments, known as "tables," shall lie longitudinally between the players. One of these is known as the "outer," the other as the "inner" or "home" table. Which of the two is for the time being the inner and which the outer table is governed by the arrangement of the men at starting.
entries.note: Player-relative structure only: two tables a side, inner and outer, twelve points each. Which physical compartment is which is a separate fact - see inner-table-handedness.

entries.name: How the twenty-four points are named and numbered

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / The Board and Men / p. 272

entries.evidence: Each table is marked with twelve "points," six at either end. ... The two points in the inner table farthest from the dividing partition or "bar" are known as the "ace" points, and those next in order as the two or "deuce" points, followed in succession by the three or "trois" points, the four or "quatre" points, the five or "cinque" points, and finally the "six" points, next the bar. The points in the outer tables are designated in like manner, but starting in this case from the dividing partition. The ace point in the outer table is more commonly known as the "bar" point.
entries.note: The corpus defining its own vocabulary, which is a rule and not a preamble. It is the sole authority for a board having twenty-four points and for the two numbering directions - inner tables from the far end, outer tables from the bar. Without it starting-position, enter-from-bar and every bearing-off entry are uninterpretable.

entries.name: Which physical compartment of the board is the inner table

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / The Board and Men / p. 272

entries.evidence: With the men placed as in Fig. 1, the right hand is the inner or home table, and the left hand consequently the outer table.
entries.note: The only fact in this corpus that is genuinely beyond a plain-text adapter. The rule is fully determined - but only in Fig. 1, which fixes the left/right orientation the sentence refers to. No engine that models positions player-relatively ever asks; it is recorded because the limit is real, not because it is load-bearing.

entries.name: The starting arrangement of the men

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / The Board and Men / p. 273

entries.evidence: The men are arranged at starting as shown in {273} Fig. 1--viz., two of White's men are placed on the ace point in Black's inner table, five are placed on the six point in Black's outer table, three on the deuce point in White's outer table, and five on the six point in White's inner table. Black's men are placed in like manner on the points immediately facing these.
entries.note: Stated in prose and over-determined. The pips follow from the designations in point-designations: 24(2)/13(5)/8(3)/6(5), fifteen men, mirrored by pip + (25 - pip). Footnote 67 requires exactly three men on the outer deuce point for its blot to exist, and nineteen opening lines in Hints for Play are consistent with this arrangement and no other. Previously mapped beyondAdapter/declined against Fig. 1; that was a misreading of a sentence one paragraph earlier, which is about board handedness.

entries.name: A man may be played only to a permitted point

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 273

entries.evidence: Vacant; own men; exactly one adversary man; two or more refused. And entry from the bar onto a point the entering player's own men hold, which is where this rule and enter-from-bar disagree.

ambiguity.question: Three sentences later the corpus states the destinations open to a man entering from the bar as 'a vacant point or blot', omitting this rule's second arm -- a point the player's own men hold. Either this general qualification on 'the right to move' governs entry as well and the entry sentence is shorthand for it, or entry is a stated exception to it. Each reading is internally coherent and the corpus chooses neither.

entries.note: Decided: the general rule governs entry. The reading is observable in exactly one test -- EnterFromBarTests.Entry_is_permitted_on_a_point_the_entering_players_own_men_hold -- which fails under the other one.

entries.name: A single man is a blot and may be hit

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 273

entries.name: A man on the bar re-enters before any other man moves

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 273

entries.evidence: Entry available and unavailable; all other men suspended while one is up; and entry onto a point the entering player's own men hold, which is the case the two readings differ on.

ambiguity.question: This sentence names two destinations for an entering man, 'a vacant point or blot', where legal-destination three sentences earlier names three -- it omits a point the entering player's own men hold. Either the general qualification governs entry and this is shorthand for it, or entry is narrower than ordinary movement. Read strictly, this sentence and full-table-suspension are exact negations of one another, which is what makes both readings coherent.

entries.note: Decided: the general rule governs entry, so a point the entering player's own men hold is open to him. The reading is observable in EnterFromBarTests.Entry_is_permitted_on_a_point_the_entering_players_own_men_hold, which fails under the other one.

entries.name: Play is wholly suspended against a full home table

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 273

entries.evidence: Six points held by two or more; the adversary throwing and moving alone; and six points all occupied but one of them by the entering player's own men, which suspends nobody.

ambiguity.question: 'Completely full -- i.e., each point occupied by two or more men' is unqualified, so two of the entering player's own men satisfy it. Either 'full' means full of the adverse player's men, which is the only reading consistent with the general rule governing entry, or it means occupied by anyone, which is the exact negation of enter-from-bar's 'a vacant point or blot'. The corpus determines both readings and chooses neither.

entries.note: Decided: 'full' means adversely full. The reading is observable in FullTableSuspensionTests.A_point_held_by_the_entering_players_own_men_does_not_make_the_table_full, which fails under the other one. The same decision settles whether both players can be suspended at once through play: under this reading they cannot, so the engine's UnsupportedInteraction for that position answers only what a caller may assert.

entries.name: The whole throw must be played if it can be

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 273

entries.evidence: A throw fully playable, partly playable, and unplayable.

ambiguity.question: An unplayable part is lost and the whole must be played 'if it is possible'. The text does not say what happens when either die alone is playable but not both -- a case every modern ruleset settles explicitly.

entries.note: status and ambiguity.fate are independent (docs/decisions/0005), so an engine may implement this rule and still decline the case the question names -- which is the whole of what it declines. Read as an obligation to play a set of numbers that cannot be extended, the compulsion settles every other throw from the text: doublets are never ambiguous, and a throw with one playable die compels it. Where the entry is implemented the conformance verdict covers every case but the one named, and the declining case ships WholeThrowTests.Where_either_die_alone_can_be_played_but_not_both_the_corpus_does_not_settle_it.

entries.name: An unusable number bears off from the highest occupied point

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Bearing off the Men / p. 275

entries.evidence: The six-throw example; and a usable throw, which must be played forward instead.
entries.note: Clear, correct, and the opposite of what a modern player expects: a number that neither of the two fashions can deal with bears a man off the highest occupied point even where men still stand above it, which a modern ruleset refuses. Under docs/decisions/0005 the entry names the test that fails under the assumed reading: BearingOffDetailTests.A_blocked_forward_move_bears_off_from_the_highest_point_men_still_above_it. It is the one case in the suite where Hoyle's rule and the modern rule differ.

entries.name: A win is a hit, a gammon, or a backgammon

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Bearing off the Men / p. 275

entries.evidence: All three: adversary bearing off; not yet bearing off; a man up or in the winner's home table. And the finish none of the three names.

ambiguity.question: The three named results do not cover every finish. Written as predicates on the loser they are: all his men home and he has begun to bear off (a hit); he has not begun to bear off (a gammon); he has a man up or in the winner's home table (a backgammon). A loser who has borne off a man, been taken up, re-entered and run that man clear of the winner's home table answers none of them, and the corpus does not say what such a win is worth.

entries.note: Was recorded clarity: clear, which asserts the corpus determines one answer for every valid input, while the engine returned RequiresInterpretation citing this entry -- the live violation of the correspondence table. The gap case is reachable and not a curiosity: the winner hits a bearing-off opponent's blot from outside, which he can only do while still running, and then finishes first. The declining case ships GameValueTests.The_three_named_results_do_not_cover_every_finish. A second, smaller defect stays in clear's ledger rather than in the question: the three are not disjoint either -- a loser who has borne off nothing and has a man up answers the gammon and backgammon conditions both -- so an ordering had to be chosen, backgammon first, and clear does not record that a choice was made. See finding 4 in the engine's MAP-FINDINGS.md.

entries.name: The multiple the players agreed a backgammon pays

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Bearing off the Men / p. 277

entries.evidence: Both figures the corpus admits, thrice and four times, and a figure outside them refused.
entries.note: 'The loser pays either thrice or four times (as may have been agreed) the amount of the single stake.' The corpus names a decider -- the players -- so this is a delegated standard and not a gap, and under docs/decisions/0005 the standard is its own entry with the rule that consumes it depending on it. The engine owes it the four things an assertion is owed: demand it, attribute it, record it alongside the outcome, never infer it. The corpus also bounds it, thrice or four times and nothing else, and that bound is a rule the engine keeps; reading the delegation as an ambiguity returned RequiresInterpretation and threw it away.

entries.name: What each result pays

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Bearing off the Men / p. 275

entries.evidence: All three: the single stake for a hit, double for a gammon, and for a backgammon the agreed multiple, which does not vary what the other two pay.
entries.note: The figures the corpus states, with the delegated one split out into agreed-backgammon-multiple under docs/decisions/0005. Nothing here is unclear: a hit pays the single stake and a gammon double, and for a backgammon the corpus names the players as the decider rather than failing to decide. Was recorded clarity: ambiguous with fate: unresolved, which its own note already contradicted -- 'an assertion, not a gap'.
